title: The Pale Choir
premise: Ines Montrose, a pest controller who has spent two decades rationalizing the impossible sounds in their family's ancestral house, is summoned home when every mirror begins reflecting the room one second late. The delay is a countdown: each night the lag grows, and when it reaches a full minute, something called the Pale Choir will finish 'learning' the family's faces and take them. Ines must overcome a lifetime of trained invisibility and a bitter estrangement from their sister Odile to get everyone out before the count completes. In the end, Ines realizes the Choir can only claim those whose reflections it has fully memorized, and they stay behind as the mirror catches up, trading themselves for the family, becoming the newest voice in the count.
about_author: Juniper Sterling is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent years documenting houses that refused to behave like houses. They write horror about families trapped by inheritance, and they still refuse to hang mirrors in hallways.

chapters.title: The Call You Can't Decline
chapters.summary: Ines, working pest control in a distant city, receives a voicemail from their sister Odile: come home, the house is doing it again. POV Ines. The beat is dread disguised as annoyance; twenty years of distance collapse in one ninety-second message.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside
chapters.summary: Ines arrives to find greasy handprints on the interior of sealed windows, high up where no one could reach. Odile's teenage son Theo has been charting them. POV Ines. The emotional beat: professional skepticism cracking against evidence shaped exactly like a hand.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Ines notices the hallway mirror lags—a glass of water set down appears in the reflection a heartbeat after it stops moving. They time it: one second. POV Ines. The beat is cold vertigo; the rationalist's toolkit finally finds something it cannot explain away.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile reveals she has kept records since childhood: the lag doubles roughly every three nights. Their grandmother's diary uses the phrase 'the count.' POV alternating Ines and Odile. The beat is reluctant alliance between siblings divided by who stayed and who fled.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Sang
chapters.summary: In the attic, Ines finds sheet music for a hymn no church claims, annotated in their grandmother's hand: 'Do not let them learn your face.' POV Ines. The beat is inheritance reimagined—not property, but a debt passed down in melody.

chapters.title: Theo Hears It First
chapters.summary: Theo admits he's been hearing humming through his bedroom wall at 3 a.m., harmonized by voices that sound almost like his own. POV Theo. The beat is adolescent bravado collapsing into genuine fear he's too proud to name.

chapters.title: Two Seconds
chapters.summary: The lag hits two seconds. Ines smashes the hallway mirror, but by morning it stands unbroken, reflecting a room that now includes a figure standing just outside frame. POV Ines. The beat: violence against the house accomplishes nothing except revealing it notices.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Left
chapters.summary: A former neighbor, Marisol Vane, tells them her family fled this street in 1987 after her father's reflection stopped matching him entirely. He was found singing in the crawlspace. POV Ines. The beat is survivor testimony—proof of an exit, and proof exits have costs.

chapters.title: Packing in Silence
chapters.summary: The family prepares to leave, but Odile refuses to abandon the house—the deed, she says, is the only thing keeping the Choir patient. Sibling war erupts over duty versus flight. POV Odile. The beat: love expressed as stubbornness, duty weaponized into paralysis.

chapters.title: Four Seconds
chapters.summary: The lag reaches four seconds. Ines realizes their own reflection has begun moving independently during the gap—reaching for things Ines hasn't touched yet. POV Ines. The beat is body horror turned inward: the self becoming an unreliable witness.

chapters.title: The Crawlspace Hymn
chapters.summary: Following the humming, Ines opens the crawlspace and finds decades of belongings arranged like pews facing a wall of old mirror shards. Something has been holding services here for generations. POV Ines. The beat is archaeological horror: the family was always its congregation.

chapters.title: Marisol's Warning
chapters.summary: Marisol calls: don't run yet. Her family ran, and the Choir followed—her father's face appeared in mirrors three states away until it finished learning him. You leave on the right night or not at all. POV Ines. The beat: hope curdling into a trap with rules.

chapters.title: Eight Seconds
chapters.summary: At eight seconds, Theo's reflection starts mouthing words during the lag. Odile finally agrees to leave—but insists on burning the house first, duty to the dead outweighing sense. POV Odile. The beat: grief masquerading as obligation, and Ines seeing it clearly for the first time.

chapters.title: The Right Night
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing the ledger with lunar dates, Ines calculates the count completes in six nights—and identifies one window, night four, when the Choir 'rests' between verses. POV Ines. The beat is grim competence: the pest controller finally treating the family as the infestation's target.

chapters.title: Sixteen Seconds
chapters.summary: The lag leaps ahead of schedule. Ines's reflection now finishes movements before Ines does. Theo stops sleeping; Odile starts humming without realizing it. POV Theo. The beat: the household unraveling as the Choir rehearses them like a choir learns parts.

chapters.title: Night Three
chapters.summary: They pack the car, but the driveway gravel rearranges overnight into a spiral pointing back at the door. Every road out of town loops back to the house on GPS. POV Ines. The beat: claustrophobic realization that geography itself has joined the count.

chapters.title: The Rest Between Verses
chapters.summary: Night four arrives. The mirrors go perfectly, eerily still—the promised rest. But as they load the last bag, Ines sees their reflection remain behind in the glass, watching the others go. POV Ines. The beat: sacrifice crystallizing; the Choir wants a soloist, not a chorus.

chapters.title: Thirty-Two Seconds
chapters.summary: Ines sends Odile and Theo off alone and stays, telling them the lag resets if one voice remains to keep singing. It's half true. POV Odile, watching the house shrink in the rearview. The beat: love against duty resolved by deception—duty performed so love can escape.

chapters.title: The Soloist
chapters.summary: Alone, Ines confronts the Choir directly: dozens of reflections in the shard-wall, all wearing Ines's face at different ages, including one aged far beyond them. They understand the final voice is always the one who stays willingly. POV Ines. The beat is terrible clarity: inheritance means someone always pays.

chapters.title: Climax: The Count Completes
chapters.summary: The lag reaches sixty seconds. Ines sings the hymn backward, scrambling the Choir's memorization, buying the fleeing car one more hour as mirrors shatter room by room. The last mirror shows Ines's reflection step forward while Ines steps back. POV Ines. The beat: defiant, costly victory—the price paid in full view.

chapters.title: Aftermath: What Odile Kept
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Odile and Theo live in a mirrorless apartment. A package arrives: the grandmother's hymnal, mailed from the house, with a new annotation in Ines's handwriting—'It rests now. Keep the count.' POV Odile. The beat: grief braided with proof of love; survival that feels like debt.

chapters.title: Epilogue: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Years on, Theo, now grown, passes a shop window and sees himself move a half-second late. He doesn't panic. He hums three notes of the hymn, and the lag closes. Somewhere, something remembers being kept. POV Theo. The beat: inheritance accepted—the watch continues, and the price of survival is vigilance forever.
